title: Judges 7:16–25
context: Judges 7:16–25 narrates the night attack. Gideon divides the three hundred into three companies armed with trumpets, empty pitchers and torches. At the change of the watch they blow the trumpets, break the pitchers, raise the torches and shout, and the LORD turns the Midianites’ swords against one another. The army flees toward the Jordan, and Gideon calls men from Naphtali, Asher, Manasseh and finally Ephraim to cut off the retreat. The Ephraimites capture and kill the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb. Later Scripture remembers this as “the day of Midian” (Isaiah 9:4) and “the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb” (Isaiah 10:26).

verses.text: He divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put into the hands of all of them trumpets and empty pitchers, with torches within the pitchers.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon divides the three hundred into three companies, armed with “trumpets and empty pitchers, with torches within the pitchers.” Arminian readers note the creative obedience of the plan. Gideon uses ordinary objects and careful organization, trusting God to give the victory he promised rather than relying on swords.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the weapons are strikingly unmilitary, underscoring that the outcome depends on God. The treasure in clay vessels image of 2 Corinthians 4:7 is often recalled here, “that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God.” Shared ground: both traditions read the plan as a sign that God works through humble means.

verses.text: He said to them, “Watch me, and do likewise. Behold, when I come to the outermost part of the camp, it shall be that, as I do, so you shall do.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon tells his men, “Watch me, and do likewise.” Arminian readers note the example of leadership: Gideon goes first and asks the men to follow his lead. The success depends on the coordinated obedience of each man in his place, with no one acting on his own initiative.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Gideon’s confidence now rests on the word and sign God has given him, so he can lead decisively. Leadership in God’s service flows from trust in his promise. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of faithful leadership by example, and neither finds a doctrinal contrast in it.

verses.text: When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp, and shout, ‘For the LORD and for Gideon!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The men are to shout, “For the LORD and for Gideon!” Arminian readers note that the shout joins God and his chosen servant, with the LORD named first. Human agents are truly involved, and Gideon’s role is real, but it is always subordinate to the LORD’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the order: the LORD first, Gideon second. The battle cry acknowledges that Gideon is God’s instrument. Shared ground: both traditions read the cry as honoring God as the source of victory while recognizing the human servant he uses, a pattern both see throughout Scripture.

verses.text: So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outermost part of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch, when they had but newly set the watch. Then they blew the trumpets and broke in pieces the pitchers that were in their hands.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon and his hundred reach the camp “in the beginning of the middle watch,” just after the guard has changed. They blow trumpets and smash pitchers. Arminian readers note the careful timing, chosen for maximum confusion, as an example of how faith and wise planning work together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the timing, at the change of the guard, serves God’s purpose of throwing the enemy into confusion. God works through ordinary circumstances and human judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing obedient action at the right moment, through which God brings about the promised deliverance.

verses.text: The three companies blew the trumpets, broke the pitchers, and held the torches in their left hands and the trumpets in their right hands with which to blow; and they shouted, “The sword of the LORD and of Gideon!”
verses.arminianNotes: The three companies blow, break and shout, “The sword of the LORD and of Gideon!” Arminian readers note that the men’s hands are full with torches and trumpets, so no hand is free for a sword. The “sword of the LORD” is the decisive weapon, and the men’s part is to obey and proclaim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cry as echoing the dream’s interpretation, “the sword of Gideon” (7:14), now placed under the LORD’s name. The victory belongs to God first. Shared ground: both traditions read the scene as a dramatic illustration that the battle is the LORD’s, a principle later voiced in Zechariah 4:6: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.”

verses.text: They each stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran; and they shouted, and put them to flight.
verses.arminianNotes: “They each stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran.” Arminian readers note that the three hundred stand firm while the enemy flees. Their task is faithfulness in their assigned place, and God accomplishes the rest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Israelites do not advance or fight at this stage; they stand, and the enemy collapses. The victory is plainly God’s doing. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s people are called to stand firm in obedience, trusting him for the outcome.

verses.text: They blew the three hundred trumpets, and the LORD set every man’s sword against his fellow and against all the army; and the army fled as far as Beth Shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel Meholah, by Tabbath.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator says “the LORD set every man’s sword against his fellow and against all the army.” Arminian readers note that the decisive act is attributed directly to God. Israel’s obedience provided the occasion, but the enemy’s confusion and self-destruction came from the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the direct divine agency: God turns the enemy against itself, governing even the actions of those who oppose him. Shared ground: both traditions read this as the heart of the battle narrative, where God alone gives the victory, and both see it as a pattern recalled by later Scripture as “the day of Midian” (Isaiah 9:4).

verses.text: The men of Israel were gathered together out of Naphtali, out of Asher, and out of all Manasseh, and pursued Midian.
verses.arminianNotes: Men from Naphtali, Asher and all Manasseh are gathered to pursue Midian. Arminian readers note that the wider Israel joins in once God has given the victory. The three hundred did not need them to win, but there is now a place for many to share in the pursuit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Israelites who were not among the three hundred now take part in completing the rout. God’s reduction of the army made the source of victory plain, and now the wider people take part. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God’s people sharing in a victory he has already secured.

verses.text: Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, “Come down against Midian and take the waters before them as far as Beth Barah, even the Jordan!” So all the men of Ephraim were gathered together and took the waters as far as Beth Barah, even the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon sends messengers to Ephraim to seize the waters “as far as Beth Barah, even the Jordan,” cutting off the escape. Arminian readers note Gideon’s strategic leadership in drawing in another tribe. The pursuit requires real effort and coordination even after the decisive victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s victory is followed by faithful human work to complete it. Gideon involves Ephraim, a leading tribe, which will matter in 8:1–3. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the pursuit narrative, showing cooperation among the tribes after God has broken the enemy’s power.

verses.text: They took the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at Oreb’s rock, and Zeeb they killed at Zeeb’s wine press, as they pursued Midian. Then they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon beyond the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: The Ephraimites capture and kill the princes Oreb and Zeeb, and the places where they died bear their names. Arminian readers note that Ephraim’s part in the victory is real and significant, and those place names became lasting memorials of God’s deliverance. Gideon’s call to Ephraim gave the tribe a real share in the victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that later Scripture recalls these events as God’s acts of judgment: “Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb” (Psalm 83:11) and “the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb” (Isaiah 10:26). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the war narrative in its setting, and both see later Scripture treating it as a paradigm of God’s deliverance.
